title: Senate passes bipartisan energy permitting bill 62-33, speeds approvals for AI data centers
subtitle: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act accelerates data-center and power-plant permits, requires data centers to pay for the power they use, and now heads to the House with Sierra Club and major environmental groups in opposition.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The US Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on Thursday, November 19, 2026, by a 62-33 margin. Fourteen Democrats and one Independent joined most Republicans. The bill speeds federal permitting for data centers and power plants and includes a clause, backed by co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, requiring data centers to pay for the power they use rather than socialize costs onto other ratepayers. President Trump publicly urged Congress to pass it. The bill now moves to the House.

The vote matters because it is the first major piece of AI-adjacent legislation to clear a full chamber this cycle. The last year of IMF and NPR reporting has been about the grid shortfall — AI data-center load projected at 9.3 gigawatts of unmet demand — and the policy fight has been about who pays. Whitehouse's ratepayer clause is the mechanism that answers that question for the first time in federal law. Environmental opposition is significant: the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation argue the bill weakens accountability for both data centers and fossil-fuel projects that will supply them, and Sen. Jeff Merkley called it 'a bad deal.' The House path is not clean, and the final text may shift.

This is distinct from the GRID Act that Senators Hawley and Blumenthal introduced in February, which would have required new data centers to generate their own power separate from the grid. There is no evidence that the GRID Act was folded into the November package, and the two approaches are different: GRID isolates the data-center load entirely, while the new bill lets them connect but makes them pay. The practical effect, if the House passes something similar, is that hyperscalers can site faster but their bill for the power they induce becomes a line item the public utility commissions can enforce.

For learners: the AI story and the energy story are now the same story. Every frontier model you have heard about this year is a demand signal on the grid, and every data center announcement is a load the local utility has to cover. If you work in or near AI, the regulatory frame to track in 2027 is not AI safety law but electricity policy — because that is where the actual constraint on scaling lives.
